# Decision Record

Why Danny is shaped the way it is. Read this before reopening a settled
question. Format: decision, date, status, reasoning, what would change it.
Superseded decisions are marked, not deleted.

---

## ADR-001 — Native SwiftUI app, project generated by XcodeGen

**2026-09 · Accepted**

A download manager lives in the menu bar and the background for hours; native
SwiftUI gives the lowest resource use and the macOS look the product depends
on. `project.yml` is the source of truth and the `.xcodeproj` is generated, so
project changes review as small YAML diffs and never merge-conflict.

## ADR-002 — macOS 26 only

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

Liquid Glass is the design, and it only exists on macOS 26. Supporting older
systems meant a second, uglier look behind `#available` checks in every glass
view — code to maintain for users the design doesn't serve. A new app can pick
its baseline.

**Would change it:** a large share of users asking for macOS 15.

## ADR-003 — yt-dlp runs as a child process, not a library

**2026-09 · Accepted**

yt-dlp is Python and changes weekly as sites change. Running it as an
executable keeps Python out of the app, lets it update independently, and
contains its crashes. Danny talks to it through its CLI and a progress template.

## ADR-004 — Plugins run out of process and speak JSON over stdio

**2026-09-27 · Accepted · designed in M2**

Extractors and engines are separate executables that Danny launches and talks
to with JSON messages over stdin/stdout — the same way it already drives yt-dlp.

- **Any language** — Python, Go, Rust, Swift, JS; contributors don't need Xcode.
- **Isolation** — a plugin crash or hang can't take the app down; it can be killed.
- **No code-signing traps** — loading third-party code into a hardened, signed
  app requires disabling library validation; separate processes don't.
- **Any license** — a plugin can be open or closed source; the protocol is the contract.

Rejected: in-process bundles (signing, crashes), JavaScriptCore scripts (can't
do what yt-dlp does), XPC services (macOS-only tooling for contributors).

## ADR-005 — libmpv for playback

**2026-09-27 · Accepted · lands in M3**

Streamed torrents are mostly MKV with HEVC/AV1 and multiple audio/subtitle
tracks. AVPlayer can't open MKV at all. libmpv (via MPVKit) plays everything,
renders with Metal, and costs roughly 20 MB of app size — worth it for a
streaming feature that otherwise fails on most files.

## ADR-006 — Torrent engine as a helper process

**2026-09-27 · Open — decided by an M3 spike**

Same boundary as plugins (ADR-004). Candidates: **librqbit** (Rust, has an HTTP
streaming server built in) and **anacrolix/torrent** (Go, mature streaming
reader). The spike measures memory, CPU while seeding/idle, and time-to-first-frame.

## ADR-007 — `development` → `main`, squash in, merge out

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

Feature PRs squash into `development` (the PR title becomes the commit and the
changelog line); releases go `development` → `main` with a merge commit so the
tag sits on the released commit. Nobody pushes to either branch directly.

## ADR-008 — Resource use is a feature

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

Idle Danny costs 0% CPU; downloading costs low single digits. No always-on
timers or animations, effects drawn by Metal shaders, updates throttled, work
stopped when the window is hidden. Changes that add animation or background
work measure it. Rules: [engineering.md](engineering.md) §Danny is light.

## ADR-009 — Clean as you go

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

The first version was built fast. Rather than a rewrite, every PR leaves what it
touches cleaner, and larger debt is recorded in [backlog.md](backlog.md) and paid
down as its own PRs. The M2 core split is the one planned structural change.

## ADR-010 — Ship outside the App Store: Developer ID + notarization, no sandbox

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

Danny runs child processes it didn't build (yt-dlp, ffmpeg, plugins — ADR-003/004),
updates yt-dlp on its own schedule, and saves wherever the user points it. The App
Sandbox forbids or cripples all three, so the Mac App Store is out. Distribution is
a DMG and zip on GitHub Releases, signed with a Developer ID, hardened runtime,
notarized and stapled — what Gatekeeper expects from apps outside the store.

Builds made without signing credentials are ad-hoc signed and not notarized, and
their release notes say so. Signed, notarized releases are required before 1.0.

## ADR-011 — Homebrew: our own tap first, the official cask once notarized

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

`brew install --cask` is how many Mac developers install apps. The official
`homebrew/cask` repo requires apps that pass Gatekeeper and projects notable enough
to meet its criteria, so Danny starts in `orpheus-ui/homebrew-tap` (bumped by the
release workflow) and moves to `homebrew/cask` once both hold. docs/releasing.md.

## ADR-012 — Bundled tools are pinned, verified and native

**2026-09-27 · Accepted**

Releases bundle yt-dlp and ffmpeg so Danny works without Homebrew. Both are
pinned to exact versions and checksum-verified before bundling
(`scripts/fetch-dependencies.sh`; ffmpeg's source, ADR-013), so a release contains
exactly what was reviewed and a compromised download fails the build. ffmpeg is a
universal binary built from native arm64 and x86_64 builds — no Rosetta
dependency, which Apple is phasing out. Bumps are their own PRs.

## ADR-013 — Bundled ffmpeg: built from source, LGPL only

**2026-10-11 · Accepted**

Danny bundles its own ffmpeg and ffprobe, built by `scripts/build-ffmpeg.sh` from
the pinned, checksummed source release. The build starts from
`--disable-everything` and enables only what yt-dlp asks of ffmpeg: stream-copy
merging and remuxing, the HLS/DASH fixups, MP3 (LAME) and AAC audio extraction,
thumbnails, subtitles, metadata, and HLS over HTTPS for the streams yt-dlp hands
to ffmpeg — with TLS from macOS, so there is no TLS library to ship or patch.
Nothing GPL or nonfree goes in, so the binaries are LGPL-2.1+; their license
texts and where their source is ship inside the app
(`Contents/Resources/bin/licenses`), and every GitHub Release carries the exact
source archives they were built from.

The full static builds available for macOS are GPLv3 and ~160 MB as universal
binaries. This build does the same jobs at a fraction of the size, with much
less code exposed to untrusted media. `scripts/check-ffmpeg.sh` runs yt-dlp's
ffmpeg commands on small synthetic files (`Tests/Fixtures/media`) against every
build, so a build that can't do one of them never ships.

Would change if yt-dlp needs something the build leaves out: add it to the build
and a case to the check, never switch to a full build.

## ADR-014 — Site sign-in: sessions stay in WebKit, cookies reach yt-dlp per run

**2026-10-16 · Accepted**

Some videos need a signed-in user, and YouTube asks yt-dlp to sign in when it
suspects a bot. Danny signs in through the site's own login page in its built-in
browser (WebKit's default store, shared with Browser Capture). The password goes
to the site; Danny only sees the session cookies it leaves behind.

The sessions stay in WebKit's store and Danny keeps no copy. yt-dlp's `--cookies`
reads a file, so for each run Danny writes only the link's site cookies to a file
in the user's private temporary folder (mode 0600), and removes it when the run
ends. Cookies the site refreshed during the run are read back into the store
first, so the session doesn't go stale. Leftover files from a crash are removed
at launch. With no session for the link's site, no file is written.

YouTube is the exception to "signed in means cookies on every run": its links go
signed out first and use the session only when the link asks for a sign-in,
because some signed-in accounts get SABR-only streams capped at 360p. When the
session is used, a YouTube token (ADR-018) gets those accounts the normal streams.

`--cookies-from-browser` was the alternative: it reads the user's own browser,
which needs Full Disk Access for Safari or a keychain prompt for Chrome, and
hands yt-dlp every cookie the browser has. Sites are data (`SignInSite`), so a
new built-in site is one entry, and users add others by address.

Would change if yt-dlp reads cookies from a pipe or stdin: then nothing touches
the disk at all.

## ADR-015 — yt-dlp keeps itself current, outside the app bundle

**2026-10-16 · Accepted**

Sites change weekly and yt-dlp follows them; a yt-dlp bundled with a release
(ADR-012) ages until the next one, and an old yt-dlp is the most common cause of
failed downloads. Each time Danny opens, `YTDLPUpdater` asks GitHub for yt-dlp's
latest release and, when it is newer than the copy in use, downloads
`yt-dlp_macos`, checks it against the release's `SHA2-256SUMS`, runs it once to
confirm the version, and renames it into `~/Library/Application Support/Danny/bin`.
That copy is found before the bundled or Homebrew one, unless a newer Danny
bundled a newer yt-dlp: each copy's version sits beside it in `yt-dlp.version`,
so the choice at launch reads two small files instead of running two binaries.

The signed app bundle is never modified. The rename is atomic, so a download
already running keeps the old binary and the next one uses the new. One request
at launch and nothing while idle (ADR-008). Settings › Engine & Updates turns it off.

Accepted risk: the checksum file comes from the same GitHub release as the
binary, so it proves the download is intact, not who made it. Someone able to
change yt-dlp's releases could ship a binary that passes, and Danny runs it
(the version check) before installing it. Users who install yt-dlp from GitHub
or Homebrew take the same trust today. Verifying `SHA2-256SUMS.sig` against
yt-dlp's signing key, bundled with Danny, closes it (backlog).

Would change if yt-dlp becomes a plugin (M2): the plugin host updates plugins,
and this moves there.

## ADR-016 — QuickJS-ng is the JavaScript runtime yt-dlp uses

**2026-10-17 · Accepted**

yt-dlp needs a JavaScript runtime to read YouTube's player; without one it falls
back to a single client and a thin format list. A Mac has no runtime of its own,
so Danny bundles one and pins yt-dlp to it (`--no-js-runtimes --js-runtimes
quickjs:<path>`), so a run never depends on what else is installed.

yt-dlp supports Deno, Node, Bun and QuickJS. QuickJS-ng wins on weight: one
2.4 MB universal binary against 100 MB or more for Deno or Node. Bun is deprecated
by yt-dlp's solver and capped at 1.3.14. Deno's runtime is in a maintenance-only
period with an announced end of development. Measured on a real player with
yt-dlp's own solver, QuickJS-ng takes about 2 s the first time it sees a player
version and about 0.2 s afterwards, since yt-dlp caches the processed player;
Deno takes 0.3 s. The runtime runs only while a link is read, never while idle
(ADR-008), so the extra seconds on a new player version are the whole cost.

QuickJS-ng releases publish no checksums, so `scripts/fetch-dependencies.sh` pins
the SHA-256 of each architecture's binary, recorded when the version is bumped.
It is MIT licensed; the license text ships in `Resources/bin/licenses`.

Would change if QuickJS-ng becomes too slow for YouTube's player, or if a
YouTube token provider needs a specific runtime.

## ADR-017 — No built-in player: Play opens the user's player

**2026-10-17 · Accepted**

Danny has no video player of its own. Play opens a finished file in the app the
Mac has set for its type (IINA, VLC, QuickTime Player), and Space shows it in
Quick Look. A streamed torrent (M3) works the same way: the torrent helper serves
the file over local HTTP with byte ranges, and Danny opens that URL in the user's
player, which already handles MKV, HEVC, subtitles and seeking.

A player that matched those would mean bundling libmpv or VLCKit, tens of
megabytes plus its own updates and codec bugs, against ADR-008. AVKit adds no
weight but cannot play MKV, the usual torrent container, so it would still need
the hand-off. Playing a site download before it finishes is not offered: yt-dlp
fetches video and audio separately and merges them at the end, so the file is not
playable until then.

Would change if a common container stops opening in the players Macs ship with
or users install, or if streaming needs controls a hand-off cannot give.

## ADR-018 — YouTube tokens are minted in a hidden WebKit view

**2026-10-18 · Accepted**

Signed in, YouTube serves some accounts only SABR streams, which yt-dlp can't
read, so those accounts get the 360p file. yt-dlp's `web_creator` client still
gets every stream, up to 2160p, and they download only when its requests carry a
proof-of-origin (PO) token from YouTube's BotGuard. On such an account `mweb` and
`web` stay SABR-only even with a token, and `web_safari`'s HLS stops at 1080p. When a run is about to send YouTube cookies, `YouTubeTokens`
mints one: it opens a hidden `WKWebView` on a blank page with YouTube's origin and
the browser's sign-ins, reads the watch page to learn what YouTube binds the
token to (the video ID, or the account's data sync ID for sessions outside that
experiment, the same choice yt-dlp makes), runs BotGuard's challenge, mints the
token, and drops the view. yt-dlp gets it as
`--extractor-args "youtube:…;po_token=web_creator.gvs+<token>"` with `web_creator`
among its clients. A mint takes one to two seconds; the token is kept in memory for its
run, so the probe, the download and a retry share one, and no run reuses
another's, which may have been bound to a different account. Nothing runs while
idle (ADR-008), and a failed mint leaves the run as it was before.

yt-dlp's PO token guide points to provider plugins. The common one (bgutil) runs
BotGuard in Node or Deno, 100 MB or more that Danny doesn't ship (ADR-016), plus
a Python plugin and a local server or script for yt-dlp to call. WebKit is
already in Danny, runs BotGuard as the browser it was written for, and needs no
plugin: Danny passes the token on the command line.

The token doesn't get a signed-out run past YouTube's "confirm you're not a bot"
check, which comes from the connection, not the request; signed-out runs go on
without one.

Would change if yt-dlp reads tokens from a provider Danny can serve without a
plugin, or if YouTube moves the binding somewhere the watch page doesn't show.

## ADR-019 — Browser Capture blocks ads with a host list of its own

**2026-10-24 · Accepted**

Browser Capture blocks ad and tracker requests, on by default, with a switch in
Settings → Sources and "Allow ads on this site" in the capture browser's toolbar.
The rules are a `WKContentRuleList`: WebKit compiles them once, keeps them in
`WKContentRuleListStore` under an identifier named after a digest of the rules, and
blocks in its network process, so nothing of Danny's runs while idle (ADR-008). The
same hosts drop ad media (pre-roll MP4s, ad HLS) from the captured list, whether
the blocker is on or not. The sign-in window loads without the rules, since
blockers break some sign-in flows.

The list is `AdHosts`, about eighty major ad, ad-video and tracker hosts written
for Danny under its MIT license, and it changes only with app releases. EasyList
and EasyPrivacy would block more, but they are GPLv3 / CC BY-SA, and their
share-alike terms would reach a bundled, converted copy in an MIT app. Their tens of
thousands of rules also need a converter for WebKit's rule format and its rule
limit. Blocking whole hosts covers the ad servers and video ad CDNs that slow pages
and fill the captured list, which is what Browser Capture needs.

Would change if a permissively licensed list of the same quality appears, or if
missed ads become a common complaint.
